html:
This lecture has two versions. Dr. Nawaf AlShahwan — Abdominal & Pelvic Trauma review — is the new lecture for group F (Part 2 below). Dr. Reem Alyahya taught group A earlier (Part 1). Slides (black) with the lecture's speaker notes, Dr. Reem's notes (green), every gift (red — the "Trauma and Shock" midterm topic, ~190 questions, including head, chest and shock questions filed under it) and the Aldughaither summary (grey, at the end).

Part 1 — Dr. Reem Alyahya (group A, taught earlier).

Introduction

  • Trauma = injury caused by external force or violence. Leading cause of death in ages 1–44 (under 45). Disabilities exceed deaths 3:1; costs > $400 billion/year; lack of public awareness of prevention.
  • Mechanism: blunt, penetrating, thermal — predicts hidden internal damage.
TypeNotes (slides)
BluntFalls, MVAs — hidden damage, needs monitoring and imaging
PenetratingStab, gunshot — direct organ/vessel damage, infection, haemorrhage
BurnsThermal, chemical, electrical (rule of nines)
CrushMuscle damage, compartment syndrome, renal failure
BlastA combination of all types
  • Survivors may have permanent disability — prevention (road safety) is the best strategy. Mass-casualty events trigger hospital-wide activation.
  • Most important determinant in reducing injury at impact in a road accident → speed limitation. 430

Principles & ATLS

  • Goals: rapid, accurate physiological assessment · resuscitate, stabilize and monitor by priority · prepare for transfer to definitive care · teamwork for optimal, safe care.
  • ATLS — James K. Styner (1972), orthopaedic surgeon who crashed his plane; his wife died and three children were critically injured; care at the nearest hospital was inadequate → "something wrong with the system".

Trimodal death distribution

PeakTimingCause
ImmediateSeconds–minutes at the sceneCatastrophic injuries — prevention only
EarlyMinutes–hours ("golden hour")Haemorrhage — the main preventable cause
LateDays–weeks (~2–3 weeks)Sepsis, multi-organ failure

Preparation

  • Pre-hospital: closest appropriate facility, transport protocols, on-line medical direction, mobilization of resources.
  • In-hospital: preplanning, team approach, trained personnel, standard precautions, equipment, lab/X-ray, transfer agreements.
  • Standard precautions: cap, gown, gloves, mask, shoe covers, goggles/face shield.

Pre-hospital preparation · in-hospital preparation · standard precautions

  • Pre-hospital notification lets the team prepare blood, imaging and an OR. Peripheral hospitals must at least resuscitate, stabilize and transfer.
  • Life-threatening vascular injury after an RTA, nobody with him → no consent needed (emergency). 438 ×2

Primary survey — ABCDE

  • Airway + cervical spine control · Breathing and ventilation · Circulation with haemorrhage control · Disability (neurological status) · Exposure and environmental control.
Save life before limb. Priorities stay A → B → C → D → E; the primary survey identifies and treats life-threatening problems and stays "open" until ABC is controlled.
  • Aim of the primary survey → identify (and treat) life-threatening injuries 441; condition primarily assessed and managed in it → hypoxia 442; correct order → airway with c-spine, breathing, circulation. 430
  • Must be ruled out in the primary survey → open pneumothorax 431 ×3; most often missed in the primary survey → cardiac contusion. 437

A — Airway with C-spine control

  • Assess patency — snoring, gurgling, stridor; maxillofacial/laryngeal injury; chin lift / modified jaw thrust; look, listen, feel; remove particulate matter; definitive airway as necessary.
  • Simplest test: can the patient speak? Definitive airway = cuffed tube through the vocal cords (ETT) — an LMA or mask is not. Protect the C-spine (collar) until injury is excluded. Signs of obstruction: stridor, hoarseness.
GCS ≤ 8 → intubate (can't protect the airway). Suspected C-spine injury → jaw thrust (no head tilt), in-line immobilization while securing the airway.
  • Snoring unresponsive footballer / maxillofacial fracture → open the airway with a jaw thrust 432 ×3 432 438 ×3; fall from height, needs airway → in-line immobilization and a definitive airway. 438 ×6
  • Severe maxillofacial injury, can't intubate → cricothyroidotomy 432 ×5; unconscious stabbed man → endotracheal intubation 432 ×4; GCS 7 / GCS 6 → intubate. 439 431
  • Agitated, bloody secretions in the mouth, respiratory distress, bleeding femur → first suction the mouth (rigid catheter) 438 ×5; raccoon eyes with nasal bleeding → immediate threat airway obstruction. 429 ×2
  • Electrical burn + 3-m fall, unconscious → intubation. 437 ×2
  • Haematemesis — first step → airway (ensure/secure it) 438 ×5 438 ×3

B — Breathing

  • Inspect chest rise and symmetry · palpate · percuss · auscultate breath sounds · O₂ saturation · rate/effort · colour/sensorium.
  • Hyperresonance → pneumothorax; dullness → haemothorax. Subcutaneous emphysema in trauma = pneumothorax until proven otherwise. ~4 minutes of severe hypoxia damages the brain.
  • Unrestrained driver — key breathing finding → breath sounds. 438 ×3
Tension pneumothorax is a clinical diagnosis — decompress immediately, no X-ray first. Needle in the 2nd intercostal space, mid-clavicular line (ATLS 10 now advises the 4th–5th ICS anterior/mid-axillary line in adults), then a chest tube.
  • Tracheal deviation, hyperresonance/absent breath sounds, hypotension → tension pneumothorax 439 437 — an obstructive shock 442 434; after a subclavian line → tension pneumothorax. 438 ×3
  • Trachea to the left, right chest hyperresonant → needle decompression, 2nd ICS MCL, right side 442; agitated, hypotensive after MVA → needle decompression 434 ×2 430 431; site → 2nd ICS mid-clavicular line 436 ×4; irrelevant in tension pneumothorax → "confirm chest-tube position with CT". 438
  • Chest tube site → 4th–5th ICS (above the 5th rib), mid-axillary line — level of the nipple, in the safe triangle 437 ×2 427 435; inserted with full aseptic technique 436; not an indication → pneumoperitoneum. 437
  • Small traumatic pneumothorax, stable → observation with oxygen 442; stab wound with a small pneumothorax and moderate effusion → chest tube 439; stab to the right chest, BP 80/40 → chest tube (haemothorax). 438 ×5
  • Chest tube drains 1600 mL after a gunshot → emergency thoracotomy (massive haemothorax: > 1500 mL initially or > 200 mL/h). 439
  • Open (sucking) chest wound → three-sided dressing 431, then a chest tube away from the wound. 430
  • Flail chest — the false statement → "managed by thoracotomy" (analgesia, oxygen, ventilation if needed). 427
  • Blunt chest injury, hypotension, distended neck veins, muffled heart sounds (Beck's triad) → pericardiocentesis 442 ×2; chamber most injured by penetrating trauma → right ventricle (most anterior). 437
  • Stab to the chest, loses pulse in the ER → emergency (resuscitative) thoracotomy 441; pulseless on arrival, pulse 5 minutes ago → keyed emergency thoracotomy (written "thoracostomy"). 442
  • Stab to the neck, stable, subcutaneous emphysema + expanding haematoma (hard signs) → emergency neck exploration. 439 ×2

C — Circulation & haemorrhage control

  • Heart rate, BP, organ perfusion, level of consciousness, skin colour, pulse rate/character. Look for blood in: chest, abdomen, long bones (pelvis) and on the floor.
Hypotension in trauma is haemorrhagic shock until proven otherwise. Haemorrhagic shock is the most common cause of death in the first hour. If there is a bleeder → STOP IT (pressure, OR). Beware: elderly, pregnant, medications (β-blockers), athletes.
  • Hidden blood: haemothorax ~2 L per side, abdomen/pelvis 3–4 L, femur 1.5–2 L (bilateral femurs alone → class III). A talking patient has SBP ≈ ≥ 90. Don't progress past C until bleeding is controlled.

  • Tachycardic with normal BP after an RTA → class II 430; what the shock class reflects → the amount of intravascular volume loss. 431
  • Access: two large-bore IV lines 431; difficult peripheral access → intraosseous 432 ×2; venous cut-down → long saphenous vein anterior to the medial malleolus. 436 ×2 427
  • Fluid of choice → isotonic crystalloid — keyed 0.9% saline in one recall, Ringer's lactate in others 442 441 434 ×2 431 ×3 430; crush/extraction → 1 L Ringer's bolus. 438 ×7
  • Best guide to resuscitation → urine output 434 ×5 431 ×3; marker of occult hypoperfusion → lactate 438 ×2; MAP for 80/50 → 60. 438 ×2
  • Analgesia in a shocked polytrauma patient → IV (poor absorption from muscle/skin in shock). 438 ×7

Blood & massive transfusion (from past exams)

  • No time for cross-match → O negative 442; massive transfusion = one blood volume in 24 h 431 ×2; ratio → 1:1:1 (RBC:plasma:platelets) 442; after 6 units of packed cells → add FFP 441 ×2; in massive bleeding we ideally transfuse → whole blood. 426
  • Drug proven to reduce trauma mortality → tranexamic acid (within 3 h). 432 ×2
  • Massive transfusion complications → citrate toxicity (hypocalcaemia) 431 ×3 426; hyperkalaemia 431 ×2; ABO-incompatible transfusion → acute haemolytic reaction. 431 ×2
  • Fever after splenectomy and transfusion for haemorrhagic shock → bacterial translocation from the bowel. 432 ×2

D — Disability

  • Baseline neurological evaluation · Glasgow Coma Scale.
EyeVerbalMotor
4 spontaneous5 oriented6 obeys
3 to sound4 confused5 localizes
2 to pressure3 words4 withdraws (normal flexion)
1 none2 sounds3 abnormal flexion (decorticate)
1 none2 extension (decerebrate)
1 none
  • Minimum GCS is 3 (never 2). ≤ 8 = severe (can't protect the airway); 9–12 moderate; 13–15 mild.
  • GCS = best eye, verbal and motor responses 430 ×3; no eye opening (1) + incomprehensible sounds (2) + extension (2) → 5 437 ×4; eyes to pain (2) + sounds (2) + flexion (3) → 7 431 ×2; eyes to voice (3) + confused (4) + obeys (6) → 13. 426
  • Leading cause of death and disability in trauma → head injury. 432 ×4

E — Exposure

  • Completely undress, remove helmet, look for visible/palpable injuries, log roll (protect the spine), prevent hypothermia (warm blankets, warm fluids).

Adjuncts to the primary survey

  • Monitor: vital signs, ABG, ECG, pulse oximetry, urinary output. Diagnostic: chest and pelvis X-ray, FAST, DPL.
  • FAST = bedside US for free fluid (part of the primary survey). DPL — rarely used now; 1 L saline, positive with gross blood, enteric content, WBC > 500/mm³.
  • FAST examines 4 areas (pericardial, Morison's pouch/hepatorenal, splenorenal, pelvis) 432 ×4; FAST can't see the pancreas 439 ×2; E-FAST can't see retroperitoneal haemorrhage. 431
  • DPL — absolute contraindication → an indication for laparotomy already exists (expanding abdomen after a chest stab) 431; DPL — the false statement. 427

Secondary & tertiary survey

  • Start after: primary survey completed, resuscitation in progress, ABCDEs reassessed, vital functions returning to normal.
  • Head-to-toe examination + AMPLE history: Allergies, Medications, Past history, Last meal, Events. Transfer if needed.
  • Adjuncts: blood tests, urinalysis, CT, US, angiography, echocardiography, bronchoscopy.
  • Never send an unstable patient to CT.
  • Tertiary survey: full examination + imaging to catch injuries missed on admission (~24 h, once stable — adrenaline and pain mask small injuries).
  • Stable after an assault with a head injury → haemodynamic and neuro-vital monitoring 437; subdural haematoma + other injuries → advanced haemodynamic monitoring and neuro-status 436; who benefits most from ICU → young man with multiple head and trunk injuries. 438

Trauma triad of death & damage control

Lethal triad: coagulopathy · acidosis · hypothermia.
  • "Triad of death" → acidosis, hypothermia and coagulopathy. 439
  • Damage control — 3 stages: 1. OR — stop bleeding/contamination; 2. ICU — resuscitate; 3. definitive treatment.
  • Stage 1: ligate/pack, staple bowel in discontinuity, temporary closure → stage 2: warm, correct acidosis and coagulopathy → stage 3: back to OR for definitive repair.
  • After massive resuscitation: distension, falling urine output, rising airway pressures → abdominal compartment syndrome. 442

Special populations

  • Elders: 5th leading cause of death; diminished reserve; comorbidities, medications (β-blockers mask tachycardia); outcome depends on early aggressive care.
  • Children: leading cause of death; immature anatomy; vigorous physiological response, limited reserve — normal vitals until they crash.
  • Pregnancy: changes modify the response; fetal assessment; 1st priority = maternal resuscitation. Gestation and uterine position · physiological anaemia · ↓ PCO₂ · ↓ gastric emptying · supine hypotension.
  • Maternal death is the leading cause of fetal death. Don't withhold CT if needed. Left lateral tilt relieves IVC compression.
  • Pregnant woman with a large bleed yet stable → her increased stroke volume (cardiac output and blood volume ↑) 442; another version keyed increased heart rate. 437
  • Third-trimester trauma on a spine board → tilt to the left (relieve aortocaval compression). 439

Abdominal trauma

  • Spleen — the most injured organ in blunt abdominal trauma. Pain/tenderness epigastrium and left flank; Kehr's sign (left shoulder pain); hypovolaemic shock.
  • Diagnosis: FAST — if unstable go to OR; CT if stable.
GradeSubcapsular haematomaLaceration
I< 10% surface area< 1 cm depth
II10–50%1–3 cm
III> 50% or expanding> 3 cm
IVMajor devascularization (> 25% of spleen)
VCompletely shattered spleen
  • Management: operative if unstable or in a hospital with minimal capabilities; non-operative — embolization, observation.
  • Stable → observation with serial vitals/Hb, monitored bed, blood bank and immediate OR backup; ongoing bleeding (blush) → angioembolization. Stability, not grade, decides. Liver injury is managed the same way.
  • Most injured organ in blunt abdominal trauma → spleen 442 ×2 442 ×2; car crash on her left side with left rib fractures → splenic laceration. 439
  • Splenic laceration 2 cm → grade II 441; liver laceration 2 cm → grade II 442; subcapsular haematoma < 10% → grade I. 439
  • Stable blunt splenic injury with a contrast blush → angioembolization 439; grade IV with extravasation, stable after resuscitation → non-operative with angioembolization 437; stable grade III liver injury with extravasation → angioembolization 439; stable grade II liver injury → admit, serial CBC. 439
  • Non-operative splenic management contraindicated in → a peripheral hospital (no ICU/blood bank/OR backup) 437; unstable with haemoperitoneum and a 3.5–4-cm splenic laceration → total splenectomy. 436 437
  • A year after splenectomy, sepsis → Streptococcus pneumoniae (OPSI). 438 ×2

Who goes to theatre?

Unstable + positive FAST → laparotomy. Stable → CT. Peritonitis, evisceration, gunshot with instability → laparotomy regardless.
  • Gunshot to the abdomen, unstable, rigid → emergency laparotomy 442; blunt trauma, stable but peritonitis → laparotomy 442; stab, positive FAST and peritonitis though stable → laparotomy 441; epigastric stab, massive transfusion activated → open laparotomy 439; FAST positive in all 4 quadrants despite fluids and blood → laparotomy. 439
  • Blunt trauma, stable, FAST positive → CT with contrast 442; stable penetrating trauma → CT with IV contrast 441; responded to fluids, RUQ and chest tenderness → CT abdomen. 438 ×3
  • Hypotensive with a distended abdomen, resuscitation finishing → next FAST (key fixed). 442
  • Stable stab wound with evisceration → antibiotics (ceftriaxone + metronidazole) and laparotomy. 437

Hollow viscus, duodenum & bladder

  • High-speed MVA, seatbelt sign, free pelvic fluid → small bowel 439; intestinal injury → keyed can be missed on CT and treated by resection/anastomosis (if > 50% or destructive). 437
  • Child hit by the handlebar, pain and can't eat → duodenum 439; 10-year-old with a duodenal haematoma, stable → NPO + NG decompression. 442
  • Cystogram after MVA (image) → extraperitoneal bladder injury. 438
  • Blood at the meatus → retrograde urethrogram before any catheter 429; boy with a straddle injury, urethral bleeding and difficulty voiding → ascending urethrogram (key fixed). 436

Pelvic fractures

Unstable pelvis → pelvic binder/sheet first. Bleeding is mostly venous (presacral plexus) — packing; arterial → angioembolization. Unstable + positive FAST → laparotomy + pre-peritoneal pelvic packing.
  • Pedestrian, hypotensive, pelvic injury → apply a pelvic binder 438 ×4; pelvic crepitus + enlarging perineal haematoma → wrap the pelvis with a sheet 438 ×3 434
  • Pelvic fracture, FAST negative, still bleeding → retroperitoneal bleeding from the pelvis 442; open-book fracture still bleeding despite the binder → keyed venous. 442
  • Unstable pelvis, binder, FAST positive → laparotomy and pelvic packing. 439 439

Vascular injury

Hard signs → surgery: pulsatile bleeding, expanding haematoma, absent pulses, bruit/thrill, distal ischaemia. Soft signs (diminished pulse, stable haematoma, nerve deficit, proximity) → CT angiography / ABI.
  • Hard sign → active pulsatile bleeding / expanding haematoma 442; bruit or thrill 441; gunshot to the arm — finding needing urgent angiography → diminished distal pulses. 432 ×3
  • Penetrating thigh wound: stable, non-expanding haematoma, weak pulses (soft signs) → CT angiography. 442
  • Posterior knee dislocation → popliteal artery injury 439; after revascularization of an ischaemic leg → hyperkalaemia (reperfusion). 436

Abdominal & pelvic trauma review — Dr. Nawaf AlShahwan (group F)

Part 2 — the new lecture for group F (2026 slides). Case-based review by Dr. Nawaf AlShahwan, Trauma Director at KSUMC (acute care surgeon, trauma surgeon and intensivist). Outline: penetrating torso injuries · penetrating colonic injury · blunt splenic injury · blunt pelvic/abdominal injury · damage control surgery · abdominal compartment syndrome. The slides ask questions without an answer key; the answers in "Show the answer" are added from the slides that follow each question.

Penetrating torso injuries

Case: 25 y/o male presents to the trauma room with a left flank torso stab wound. He is hemodynamically stable with no peritonitis. His FAST exam is negative. What is the next best step? 1. Irrigate and close wound in ED · 2. Local wound exploration · 3. Immediate laparoscopy · 4. Immediate laparotomy · 5. Triple contrast CT scan

Show the answer
Added5. Triple contrast CT scan. He is stable with none of the indications for immediate laparotomy, and the wound is in the flank — flank and back wounds need a triple contrast CT (oral, IV, rectal) to rule out retroperitoneal injuries.

Immediate indications for laparotomy (penetrating torso trauma)

  • Instability.
  • Stable but has one of the following: peritonitis · evisceration · positive FAST · blood in Foley, NGT or rectum · embedded object.

Other considerations

  • Bullet rule — X-ray the torso: number of holes + number of bullets on X-rays must equal an even number.
Added explanationEach bullet either leaves (entry + exit = 2 holes) or stays (1 hole + 1 bullet on the X-ray), so an odd total means a missed wound or a missed bullet.

Location of the wound

  • 1. Anterior abdomen · 2. Thoracoabdominal · 3. Flank · 4. Back · 5. Cardiac box.
LocationWork-up
Anterior abdomenCT scan — free air, free fluid, thickened bowel, mesenteric stranding · wound exploration — peritoneal penetration
Flank / backTriple contrast CT (oral, IV, rectal) — rule out retroperitoneal injuries; kidney injury or blood in the Foley → also a delayed scan (2nd CT abdo/pelvis, no extra contrast, ~10 min after the first)
ThoracoabdominalLeft side: delayed laparoscopy (> 12 h after admission) to rule out diaphragmatic injury · right side: may need laparoscopy depending on location
Cardiac boxFAST × 2 for pericardial fluid · CT chest to rule out great-vessel injury
  • Epigastric wounds span the anterior abdomen, the thoracoabdominal area and the cardiac box.
Added explanationThe liver shields the right hemidiaphragm, so a missed left-sided diaphragm hole is the one that later lets bowel herniate into the chest — hence the routine laparoscopy on the left.
  • Gifts: stable stab wound with evisceration → antibiotics and laparotomy 437; stab with positive FAST and peritonitis though stable → laparotomy 441; stable penetrating trauma → CT with IV contrast. 441

Penetrating colonic injury

Case: 29 y/o male with multiple stab wounds to the cardiac box, left chest and left abdomen. BP 85/40, pulse 120, RR 25. FAST indeterminate for abdominal and pericardial fluid. CXR shows only a left haemothorax; a left chest tube puts out 300 cc.

  • In the operating room: an extraperitoneal pericardial window is done first — negative, then closed. At laparotomy: 1.5 L of blood in the peritoneal cavity and a large hole in the left colon with some faecal contamination.

Which statements are true about appropriate management? A. Left-sided colonic injuries should all be managed by a Hartmann's procedure. B. Resection and primary anastomosis of left-sided colonic injuries should be considered. C. Right-sided colonic injuries should all be managed by a right hemicolectomy with primary anastomosis or end ileostomy. D. Primary repair of right-sided colonic injuries should be considered. — 1. A, B and C · 2. A and C · 3. B and D · 4. D only

Show the answer
Added3. B and D. By the EAST guidelines below, non-destructive wounds get primary repair, and destructive wounds can still have resection and primary anastomosis when the patient qualifies — the side of the colon doesn't decide, so "all Hartmann's" (A) and "all hemicolectomy" (C) are wrong.

Penetrating colonic injury — EAST guidelines

  • Level 1: sufficient class I and II data support a standard of primary repair for non-destructive colon wounds (< 50% of the bowel wall without devascularization) in the absence of peritonitis.
  • Level 2: destructive penetrating intraperitoneal colon wounds (> 50% of the bowel wall or devascularization of a segment) can undergo resection and primary anastomosis if the patient is: haemodynamically stable (no sustained pre- or intra-operative SBP < 90 mmHg) · has no significant underlying disease · has minimal associated injuries · has no peritonitis.
  • Gift: intestinal injury → keyed treated by resection and anastomosis (if > 50% or destructive). 437

Blunt splenic injury

Case: 65 y/o male fell off a ladder and landed on his left side. GCS 15, haemodynamically stable. Some left lower rib fractures, small pulmonary contusion, no PTX/HTX, LUQ tenderness. CT abdomen: significant haemoperitoneum · grade 4 splenic injury · contrast extravasation · no other visceral injury and no other injuries on work-up. Four hours later the haemoglobin has fallen from 13 to 9.

Which statements are correct? A. Laparotomy with splenectomy is a reasonable next step. B. Angioembolization is a reasonable next step. C. It is reasonable to watch in ICU and repeat the CT scan. D. VTE prophylaxis is contraindicated during this admission (post-injury day 7). — 1. A, B and C · 2. A and C · 3. B and D · 4. D only

Show the answer
Added1. A, B and C. In a stable patient a grade 4 injury with a blush can be watched in ICU or embolized, and the falling Hb makes splenectomy reasonable too. D is false: EAST says pharmacologic VTE prophylaxis can be used in isolated blunt splenic injury without increasing the failure rate of non-operative management.

Why operate? Why non-operative management?

  • Why operate: 1. stop bleeding! 2. avoid missed injuries!

Uncontrolled haemorrhage · injured bowel found at laparotomy

  • Why non-operative management: 1. OPSI 2. surgical complications.
  • OPSI — overwhelming post-splenectomy infection from encapsulated bacteria (S. pneumoniae, N. meningitidis, H. influenzae): rare · younger people at higher risk · risk greatest in the 1st year post-op · risk of death in the post-splenectomy population ~0.02–0.03% in adults, ~0.3–0.6% in children · vaccine reduces the risk.
  • Gift: a year after splenectomy, sepsis → Streptococcus pneumoniae (OPSI). 438 ×2
  • Complications of trauma laparotomy: after negative trauma laparotomies, 2% SBO on long-term follow-up (n = 248, Weigelt 1988); another series (n = 80) had no SBO and no ventral hernia at a mean 3 years (Morrison 1996).
  • Ventral hernia after midline closure: polypropylene vs PDS 20.2% vs 24.2% (Bloemen 2011) · continuous vs interrupted 2% vs 0.5% (Richards 1983).

Evidence for non-operative management (NOM)

  • Pachter 1998 — 102 initially stable patients: 2% needed a later laparotomy, 15% needed transfusion, 0% mortality; average transfusion 0.8 units with NOM vs 6.0 with splenectomy. → If stable, a very high NOM rate should be seen, and NOM mortality should be very low.
  • Peitzman 2005 (EAST) — 1488 patients, 97 failed NOM. On admission 44% stable, 31% transient responders, 25% unstable. Mortality of NOM failures: overall 12.8% — stable 3%, responders 8%, unstable 37%. → Unstable patients (and transient responders?) shouldn't undergo NOM.

Splenic injury grading scale

GradeInjury

3Subcapsular haematoma > 50% or expanding; intraparenchymal haematoma > 5 cm or expanding; laceration > 3 cm deep or involving trabecular vessels
4Laceration involving segmental or hilar vessels with major devascularization (> 25% of spleen)
5Completely shattered spleen; hilar vascular injury that devascularizes the spleen
  • Gifts: splenic laceration 2 cm → grade II 441; subcapsular haematoma < 10% → grade I. 439

  • Role of angioembolization (A&E): WEST study 2004 — 140 patients (96% blunt) from 4 institutions with positive CT findings had angiography and embolization followed by NOM; success was higher than EAST without A&E for grades 3–5. It is unclear how many had active bleeding vs aneurysm vs haemoperitoneum without active bleeding.
  • Routine follow-up CT? Bradley 1997 — 108 splenic injuries, 73 (68%) NOM with routine follow-up CT (grade 1: 2, grade 2: 29, grade 3: 27, grade 4: 15, grade 5: none). Only 1 scan (2%) changed care — a grade IV injury with a pseudoaneurysm. → Follow-up CT (< 10 days) may be useful for high-grade injuries.

Current guidelines (EAST)

  • Level 1: unstable or diffuse peritonitis → emergent laparotomy.
  • Level 2: laparotomy is not indicated in stable patients without peritonitis with an isolated splenic injury · NOM needs an abdominal CT with IV contrast to grade the injury and rule out other visceral injuries · CT grade, degree of haemoperitoneum, neurologic status, age > 55 and associated injuries are not contraindications to a trial of NOM in a stable patient · angiography for AAST grade > III, a contrast blush, moderate haemoperitoneum or evidence of ongoing splenic bleeding · NOM needs monitoring, serial clinical evaluations and the capability to do an urgent laparotomy.
  • Level 3: persistent systemic inflammatory response, increasing or persistent abdominal pain, or an unexplained Hb drop dictate follow-up imaging · a contrast blush alone is not an absolute indication for operation or angiography (consider age, grade and hypotension) · angiography as an adjunct for patients at high risk of delayed bleeding, or to find pseudoaneurysms · pharmacologic VTE prophylaxis can be used without increasing NOM failure (optimal timing not determined).
  • Controversies with angiography and embolization: frequency of Hb checks and abdominal examinations · intensity and duration of monitoring · a transfusion trigger for intervention · time to restart oral intake · duration of restricted activity · length of ICU and hospital stay · need for repeat imaging · timing of chemical DVT prophylaxis · vaccines after severe or embolized injuries · immune deficiency after splenic embolization.
  • Gifts: stable blunt splenic injury with a contrast blush → angioembolization 439; grade IV with extravasation, stable after resuscitation → non-operative management with angioembolization 437; NOM contraindicated in → a peripheral hospital 437; unstable with haemoperitoneum and a splenic laceration → total splenectomy. 436

Blunt abdominal and pelvic trauma

Case: 37 y/o male, motorcycle crash — pelvic tenderness, scrotal haematoma and distended abdomen. GCS 15, BP 80/50, P 125, RR 35. CXR negative. Pelvic X-ray shows an open-book pelvic fracture.

  • Urethrogram — key points: perform with an oblique view · 10 cc undiluted Gastrografin · Foley: gentle insufflation of the balloon · inject with an immediate X-ray · a follow-up plain cystogram is helpful, especially if going to the OR.
  • FAST or DPA negative or a small amount of blood → prioritize the pelvis: external fixator, angio-embolize, ± laparotomy, ICU.
  • FAST or DPA positive → prioritize the abdomen: laparotomy + pack, ex-fix → unstable: angio; stable: ICU.
  • Gifts: pedestrian, hypotensive with a pelvic injury → apply a pelvic binder 438 ×4; unstable pelvis in a binder, FAST positive → laparotomy and pelvic packing 439; blood at the meatus → retrograde urethrogram before any catheter. 429

Damage control surgery

Case: 27 y/o male — 1 GSW to the right anterior abdomen and 1 GSW to the left upper abdomen. FAST positive, hypotensive. Injuries: liver, IVC (infrarenal), duodenum (D2, 50% of the circumference), spleen, distal pancreas, left colon. Temperature 32 °C, pH 7.05.

What will you do in the OR? A. Repair duodenum. B. Pancreatic and splenic resection. C. Pack the liver. D. Pyloric exclusion. — 1. A, B and C · 2. A and C · 3. B and D · 4. D only

Show the answer

Principles of damage control surgery

Management of the Injured Patient

Trauma is one of the most significant public health concerns in the United States and worldwide. It is the leading cause of death among people aged 1-45 and results in more lost working years than any other cause of mortality.

I. Epidemiology of Trauma
Leading cause of death in young individuals (1-45 years old)

Major contributor to elderly hospitalizations (6% of Medicare admissions) Alcohol involvement: One-third of traffic-related deaths Economic burden: Estimated cost $671 billion annually

II. Trauma Death Distribution: The Evolution from Trimodal to Bimodal

Traditionally, trauma deaths followed a trimodal distribution, but due to advancements in trauma systems, this pattern has shifted to a bimodal distribution.

A. Immediate Deaths (Seconds to Minutes)
  • Occurs at the scene of injury → Patients die before reaching the hospital.
  • Causes:
  • Massive brain or spinal cord trauma
  • Exsanguination (massive hemorrhage)
  • Survival chances: Extremely low, even with immediate care.
  • Prevention is the key strategy (e.g., seat belts, helmets, firearm control).
B. Early Deaths (Minutes to a Few Hours)
  • Occur within the first few hours post-injury.
  • 50% due to internal hemorrhage, 50% due to CNS injuries.
  • Potentially treatable with rapid intervention.
  • Key strategies to reduce mortality:
  • Rapid transport (e.g., air ambulance, trauma teams)
  • Trauma centers with immediate surgical capability
  • Early hemorrhage control (e.g., damage control resuscitation, permissive hypotension, TXA administration)
  • Advanced neurocritical care for traumatic brain injury (TBI)
C. Late Deaths (Days to Weeks)
  • Historically associated with multiple organ failure (MOF) and sepsis.
  • Now predominantly caused by refractory intracranial hypertension.
  • Key strategies for reduction:
  • Aggressive critical care (e.g., sepsis prevention, early mobility, nutritional support)
  • Advancements in neurocritical care
  • Improved infection control measures
III. Trauma Systems & Improved Outcomes
Trauma centers provide:
  • 24/7 rapid resuscitation and operating room access
  • Protocol-driven care (Advanced Trauma Life Support - ATLS)
  • Specialized teams (trauma surgeons, critical care physicians, anesthesiologists, neurosurgeons, orthopedic surgeons)

The goal of a trauma system is to minimize preventable morbidity and mortality by ensuring that injured patients receive timely, organized, and efficient care. A well-structured trauma system includes prehospital triage, rapid transport, definitive care, and rehabilitation.

Key Components of a Trauma System
  • Prehospital Care: Identification, triage, treatment, and transportation of trauma patients.
  • Trauma Triage Protocols: Standardized anatomic and physiologic criteria to identify critically injured patients.
  • Regional Trauma Centers: Coordination with EMS providers for seamless transfer and care.
  • Disaster Preparedness: Trauma centers are equipped to manage mass casualty incidents.
II. Levels of Trauma Centers (American College of Surgeons Designation)

The American College of Surgeons (ACS) classifies trauma centers into four levels, depending on capabilities and resources.

surgeons, neurosurgeons, orthopedic surgeons, plastic surgeons,
anesthesiologists, and radiologists. Includes teaching and research
obligations.

III. Trauma Triage & Field Triage Guidelines

Triage Criteria (CDC Guidelines):

1- Vital Signs & Level of Consciousness

  • Glasgow Coma Scale (GCS) ≤ 13
  • Systolic Blood Pressure < 90 mmHg
  • Respiratory Rate < 10 or > 29 breaths/min
2- Anatomic Criteria (Serious Injuries Requiring Trauma Center Care)
  • Penetrating injuries to head, neck, torso, or extremities
  • Chest wall instability or deformity (flail chest)
  • Two or more long-bone fractures
  • Crushed, degloved, or mangled extremity
  • Pelvic fractures
  • Open or depressed skull fractures
3- Mechanism of Injury & Energy Transfer
  • Falls > 20 feet (adults) or > 10 feet (children)
  • High-speed motor vehicle crashes (> 40 mph)
  • Vehicle ejection, rollover, or intrusion > 12 inches
  • Pedestrian or bicyclist struck by vehicle at > 20 mph
  • Motorcycle crash > 20 mph

Prehospital Care & Immediate Measures at an Incident Site I. Initial Response to Trauma at the Scene Trauma victims may not always exhibit visible external injuries, but a high-impact mechanism of injury should raise suspicion for severe internal trauma. The initial management priorities at the scene follow a structured approach to prevent further injury and stabilize the patient for transport.

Key Immediate Actions at the Scene

1- Assess Airway & Breathing

  • Ensure the victim is breathing.
  • If not, provide an airway (jaw thrust or chin lift) and establish bag-mask ventilation.
2- Check Circulation
  • If there is no pulse, begin closed-chest compressions (CPR).
3- Control Major Bleeding
  • Apply direct pressure and elevate the limb if possible.
  • Use a tourniquet for severe extremity bleeding (recommended for trained personnel).
4- Protect the Spine & Neck
  • Assume a cervical spine injury if the mechanism of trauma is significant.
  • Immobilize the neck and spine before moving the patient.
5- Splint Obvious Fractures
  • Stabilize any fractures or suspected dislocations before transport.
6- Prepare for Safe Transport
  • Once stabilized, transport the patient to a trauma center as quickly as possible.

Shock is defined as inadequate end-organ tissue perfusion, which can rapidly lead to multi-organ failure and death if not treated promptly.

A. Hypovolemic Shock (Most Common in Trauma)

  • burns, or severe crush injuries.

Management of Hypovolemic Shock 1. Secure Two Large-Bore IV Lines (14-16G) or IO Access 2. Fluid Resuscitation Strategy:

  • Crystalloids (Ringer’s lactate/NS) 1-2 L bolus first

3. Blood Transfusion Guidelines:

  • ≥ Class III Shock → Start O-negative or type-specific PRBCs

5. Definitive Hemorrhage Control:

  • Tourniquets for extremity hemorrhage
B. Neurogenic Shock
  • Cause: Spinal cord injury (above T6) causing sympathetic tone loss, leading
  • to massive vasodilation and pooling of blood.
  • Signs: Warm, flushed skin, hypotension, bradycardia, preserved urine
  • output.

1. IV Fluid Bolus → 2L of crystalloid first 2. If unresponsive, initiate Vasopressor Therapy:

  • Cervical spine immobilization
  • MRI & neurosurgery consultation

Cause: External compression of the heart leading to decreased venous return and cardiac output.

  • Common in Trauma: Pericardial tamponade, Tension pneumothorax, Diaphragmatic rupture.

Neck injuries can be life-threatening due to the presence of vital structures including major blood vessels, airway, spine, and esophagus. They are classified

as penetrating or blunt injuries, with distinct evaluation and treatment approaches.

Initial Assessment: Primary Survey (ABCDE)
  • Airway: Always assess for laryngeal injury, tracheal disruption, or aspiration risk.
  • Breathing: Look for tension pneumothorax, hemothorax, or pulmonary contusion.
  • Circulation: Watch for carotid or jugular vein injury leading to massive hemorrhage.
  • Disability (Neurologic): Suspect spinal cord injury in any blunt neck trauma.
  • Exposure: Fully examine the anterior and posterior neck to detect hidden injuries.
Immediate Threats to Life:
  • Airway obstruction
  • Massive hemorrhage
  • Spinal cord injury causing respiratory failure
  • Mediastinitis from esophageal injury
  • Tension pneumothorax or open pneumothorax

Management of Penetrating Neck Trauma
  • Unstable patients → Immediate surgical exploration.
  • Stable patients → Imaging & selective exploration.
  • CT Angiography (CTA) → Vascular injuries
  • Endoscopy & Esophagography → Esophageal injuries
  • Bronchoscopy → Tracheal injuries
Key Interventions
1. Airway Control
  • Endotracheal intubation (fiberoptic if possible)
  • Cricothyroidotomy or tracheostomy if laryngeal trauma.

2. Vascular Repair

  • Primary repair or vein grafting for carotid injuries.
  • Endovascular repair (stents) for selected cases.
  • Carotid artery ligation only if necessary (high stroke risk).

3. Esophageal Injuries

  • Primary repair & drainage (early repair prevents mediastinitis).
  • Broad-spectrum IV antibiotics.

4. Spinal Cord Protection

  • Maintain spinal immobilization (C-collar).
  • MRI if neurologic deficits after negative CT.
  • Early steroids are NOT recommended.

Thoracic Injuries:

Thoracic trauma contributes to 50% of trauma-related deaths due to its impact on airway, circulation, and respiratory function. Rapid identification and management of life-threatening conditions are crucial.

Initial Assessment: Primary Survey (ABCDE)
  • Airway: Secure and assess for tracheal injury, obstruction, or tension pneumothorax.
  • Breathing: Look for flail chest, pneumothorax, hemothorax, or pulmonary contusion.
  • Circulation: Identify cardiac tamponade, aortic injury, or massive hemorrhage.
  • Disability (Neurologic): Monitor for spinal cord injury or hypoxia-induced brain dysfunction.
  • Exposure: Examine for penetrating wounds, bruising, subcutaneous emphysema.
Life-Threatening Thoracic Injuries (The “Deadly Six”):

1. Airway obstruction 2. Tension pneumothorax 3. Massive hemothorax 4. Flail chest 5. Open pneumothorax 6. Cardiac tamponade

Abdominal Trauma:

Abdominal trauma is categorized into penetrating and blunt injuries. Early identification and appropriate intervention are key to preventing shock, sepsis, and multiorgan failure.

Initial Assessment: Primary Survey (ABCDE)
  • Airway: Secure airway in unstable patients.
  • Breathing: Monitor for associated thoracic injuries.
  • Circulation: Assess for hemorrhagic shock, a leading cause of death.
  • Disability (Neurologic): Identify signs of shock or brain injury.
  • Exposure: Check for seatbelt signs, bruising, penetrating wounds.
Red Flags Suggesting Abdominal Injury:
  • Unstable vitals (tachycardia, hypotension, low urine output)
  • Abdominal distension or tenderness
  • Seatbelt sign or bruising
  • Rebound tenderness, guarding (suggests peritonitis)
  • Visible penetrating injury

Vascular Trauma:

Vascular injuries pose a high risk of mortality and limb loss if not rapidly diagnosed and treated. Early identification and intervention are crucial to prevent exsanguination, ischemia, and complications like compartment syndrome.

Initial Assessment: Primary Survey (ABCDE)
  • Airway: Secure airway if unstable.
  • Breathing: Identify associated thoracic injuries.
  • Circulation: Stop bleeding immediately (direct pressure, tourniquet if needed).
  • Disability (Neurologic): Check for neurologic deficits (suggest ischemia or embolism).
  • Exposure: Identify all injury sites.
Key Red Flags for Vascular Injury:
  • Active pulsatile bleeding
  • Expanding hematoma
  • Absent or diminished pulses
  • Cold, pale, or cyanotic limb
  • Severe pain out of proportion to injury (suggests ischemia)
Types of Vascular Injuries
1- Penetrating Trauma
  • Causes: Gunshot wounds (GSWs), stab wounds, iatrogenic catheter injuries.
  • Complications: Hemorrhage, pseudoaneurysm, arteriovenous fistula (AVF).
Gunshot Wounds
  • High kinetic energy → severe tissue damage
  • More likely to cause thrombosis and embolism
  • Require imaging (arteriography or CT angiogram)
Stab Wounds
  • Lower risk of vascular injury unless deeply penetrating
  • Doppler ultrasound or angiography if vascular injury suspected
2- Blunt Trauma
  • Causes: Motor vehicle crashes, falls, crush injuries, orthopedic trauma.
  • Common Sites:
  • Thoracic aorta (high-speed crashes, deceleration injuries)
  • Popliteal artery (posterior knee dislocation)
  • Carotid & vertebral arteries (neck trauma, C-spine fractures)
Blunt Thoracic Aortic Injury (BTAI):
  • High mortality (57% die before hospital arrival)
  • Common site: Aortic isthmus (just distal to left subclavian artery)
  • Diagnosis: CT angiography of the chest
  • Management:
  • Stable: Endovascular stent graft preferred
  • Unstable: Open thoracotomy

Special Considerations
1- Compartment Syndrome
  • Occurs in 30% of vascular injuries
  • Caused by reperfusion after prolonged ischemia
  • Signs (6 P’s):
  • Pain (out of proportion)
  • Pallor
  • Pulselessness
  • Paresthesia
  • Paralysis
  • Poikilothermia (cold limb)
Fasciotomy Indications:
  • Compartment pressure >30 mmHg
  • Delayed revascularization (>6 hrs)
  • Severe swelling post-repair
2- Amputation Criteria
Immediate Amputation:
  • Nonviable limb (prolonged ischemia, necrosis)
  • Severe crush injury with mangled extremity
  • Sepsis from uncontrolled infection
  • No reconstructable vascular flow
Delayed Amputation:
  • Failed revascularization
  • Severe neuropathy with no functional recovery
  • Uncontrolled pain or infection
